asr_text: A conversation can be going well, then someone finishes a sentence, and no one answers. In one 2011 experiment, 102 undergraduate students imagined a group conversation. After a mildly controversial comment, some students read that the conversation continued normally. Others read that a brief silence followed. The silence group reported more feelings of rejection and negative emotion. They also reported less belonging, lower self-esteem, and less agreement with the group. A second experiment showed a similar pattern in a more realistic setting. In this experiment, students watched a six-minute video of a conversation. In one version, a single silence lasted four seconds. Afterward, those students reported more rejection and negative emotion, and less positive emotion and belonging. Most were not aware of the exact pause. But a long pause does not always feel bad. A 2023 study looked at natural 10-minute conversations between strangers and friends. Gaps of more than two seconds were more common among friends. For strangers, these longer gaps reduced the feeling of connection. For friends, they increased it. People who watched the conversations also judged long pauses between strangers as more awkward. The same question appears when people are alone. Across 11 studies, participants generally did not enjoy spending six to 15 minutes with nothing to do but think. They often rated simple activities as more enjoyable. In one study, 55 students sat alone for 15 minutes with the option of giving themselves a mild electric shock they had already experienced. Many chose the shock instead of remaining without outside stimulation. That was a result from this experiment, not a claim about everyone.
